content:
Nina Quirk, Culinary Services Director at The Commons in Lincoln, a Benchmark Senior Living CCRC, has been named a member of the DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards Class of 2026 by Senior Housing News.
As an Elevating the Experience Award winner, Senior Housing News recognized Quirk for her dedication, remarkable attention to detail, and positive impact on the overall service and dining experience at The Commons in Lincoln.
One of Quirk’s most meaningful contributions at The Commons is a garden project she leads in partnership with the community’s residents. Together, they plan, plant, and maintain raised garden beds filled with fresh herbs and seasonal produce. Residents are encouraged and proudly bring ingredients they have grown themselves in the garden to the culinary team, which then is incorporated into thoughtfully prepared seasonal dishes.
Another standout event under Quirk’s leadership was The Commons in Lincoln’s Spring Garden Party prospect event. Designed with a botanical theme, the event featured a thoughtfully curated menu that included elegant, edible flowers, house-infused teas, tea sandwiches, and beautifully designed desserts.
Outside of the community, Quirk was selected to present at a sold-out seminar, Wild and Foraged: A Culinary Journey, in the fall of 2025 at the prestigious Newport Mansions Wine & Food Festival. Partnering with Maria Chiancola of Newport Wine Cellar, Quirk guided attendees through the art of ethical foraging, thoughtful sourcing, and the relationship between ingredients, place, and season. She thoughtfully adapted the program for residents at The Commons, transforming the experience into an engaging educational event.
One of Quirk’s nominators told Senior Housing News, “Chef Nina Quirk’s impact on The Commons in Lincoln has been nothing short of exceptional. She is a trusted leader, a gifted and inventive chef, and passionate about always going above and beyond for the residents she serves.”
Senior Housing News recently sat down with Quirk to learn what drew her to the senior housing & senior living industry, her perspective on culinary trends, her thoughts on the future of dining in senior living, and much more. To learn more about the DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards, visit https://dishedawards.seniorhousingnews.com/.
SHN: What inspired you to pursue a career in senior living dining, and what continues to motivate your work today?
Quirk: My inspiration dates back to childhood. I had a deep connection with my grandmothers, and I wanted to be like them during my upbringing.
My paternal grandmother was a locally celebrated home chef, and her passion was passed down through many unique Italian- American food traditions.
Later in life, my husband started working in senior living administration and when I became exposed to the industry, I knew it was my pathway where food and taking care of my elders could coexist. Now, I truly enjoy listening to my residents’ food desires and bringing them to life through scratch cooking and high-quality ingredients.
SHN: What are the top three trends shaping the future of dining in senior living right now?
Quirk: The first trend I see is the need for more flexible dietary options. Residents are seeking new ways to manage complex therapeutic diets they are being prescribed for conditions, allergies, and intolerances. Senior living communities must be adaptable to the changing requirements, while maximizing enjoyment of the cuisine. This means staying a step ahead of their needs, and providing fresh, nutritious, and flavorful options.
Second, I see versatile and diverse dining spaces as a key trend. The physical spaces set the stage for the dining options provided – whether that’s restaurant-style fine dining, fast and casual dining, taverns/bars, or grab & go options – and how residents engage with their surroundings. One dining room can no longer meet all the needs of the changing clientele. Dining in a senior living environment is about socialization, connection and overall wellbeing. Meeting residents’ holistic dining needs is the primary goal, and our dining spaces must continue to evolve. The industry is even seeing more interest in dining options that are open to the public, including coffee shops, ice cream parlors and sandwich shops.
The third trend of note is increasing expectations for quality. Residents are not satisfied with frozen foods or processed foods. They request organic, grass-fed, farm fresh, local, and quality ingredients. As a dining team, you must be able to speak to all food system details, and you must cultivate reliable, high-quality sources for your dishes.
SHN: What is the biggest barrier to innovation in senior living dining today, and how can organizations effectively overcome it?
Quirk: Upgrading older facilities and kitchens to match changing marketplace demands is a huge challenge.
Newer buildings are designed with these options in mind, but as communities grow, or as buildings age, operators cannot move quickly enough to make the updates and evolve with the market demands.
Senior living organizations should look at long-term kitchen planning – back of the house and front of the house – as a priority, among other operational challenges. Planning ahead allows kitchens to perform more efficiently and effectively.
SHN: In one word, how would you describe the future of dining in senior living – and why?
Quirk: Growth.
The senior living field is growing nationally. The senior population is growing. The need for healthcare chefs is growing. The need for newer dining programs is growing. I see so much potential out there for those of us who want to grow in the industry and shape the future of senior living dining.
SHN: How do you see technology transforming dining operations and the resident experience in the next few years?
Quirk: Challenges and opportunities within the senior living dining industry will drive technology adoption. For instance, rising labor costs and a challenging job market are increasing the need for cost-controlled labor and technology has the potential to solve some of these issues.
One of the biggest trends we’ll see is self-service kiosk stations that will create a more efficient and convenient experience for many residents. We can expect to see a larger role for artificial intelligence, such as AI-assisted meal suggestions as part of the digital, self-ordering experience.
I think we will also see high-tech automated meal delivery within the community, including the use of robots or autonomous carts.
SHN: Reflecting on your career, if you could give yourself advice on your first day in senior living dining, what would it be and why?
Quirk: Residents have diverse tastes, backgrounds, cultures, and traditions, which often influence their food preferences. While you may satisfy some residents each day, others will have different expectations. Be prepared to welcome differing opinions and seize the opportunity to appreciate those differences.
SHN: What qualities or leadership traits do you think DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Award winners must embody?
Quirk: Lead with integrity in every interaction with residents and bring that same integrity to your cuisine.
True leadership is demonstrated by making resident-centered decisions and providing a dining experience that you believe in and are proud to serve. When you do this consistently, you will see how your work and creativity positively impact the lives of so many people. The fulfillment and pride that comes from what you create becomes even more meaningful.

title: Caveat emptor: How Medicare Advantage is neither Medicare nor much of an advantage

content:
Somewhere along the way, Americans collectively decided that if something has the word “Medicare” in it, it must actually be Medicare. Kind of like assuming that because “chicken fingers” contain the word chicken, they’re a healthy dinner choice. (Spoiler alert: They’re really just a vehicle for ranch dressing!)
The Romans had a phrase for this: Caveat emptor — let the buyer beware. Apparently, the Romans never had to sit through a Medicare Advantage commercial during Wheel of Fortune. If they had, they would’ve changed it to, “Let the buyer beware… especially if Joe Namath with his poorly made veneers is involved.”
Every fall, television becomes a bizarre Medicare-themed carnival. Retired football players, smiling celebrities and people who appear genuinely excited about getting free dental benefits pop up on our screens. They’re practically throwing gym memberships and grocery cards at us like beads at Mardi Gras. “You may be entitled to MORE benefits!”
More than what? That’s always my question. More restrictions? More prior authorizations? More phone calls? More hold music? More explanations about why your doctor is suddenly out of network despite having been your doctor since Reagan was president? Because yes. Sometimes all of the above.
As a nurse, I have lost count of the number of times I’ve heard someone proudly tell me, “I have Medicare.” “Wonderful,” I say. “Original Medicare?” “No. Medicare Advantage.” And that’s when I begin mentally preparing for what may become an Olympic-level event involving insurance approvals, network restrictions, denials for stay even though the resident is clearly not safe to go home, and enough paperwork to kill an entire forest.
What advantage?
Here’s the part that drives me absolutely crazy: Medicare Advantage isn’t Medicare. It’s private insurance. Let me say that again for the people in the back who are busy clipping coupons from their insurance company’s mailer.
Medicare Advantage is private insurance that Medicare pays to manage your healthcare. It’s Medicare outsourcing its homework to private companies (who have to answer to stockholders) and hoping they do a nice job. And “Advantage?” Well, that depends entirely on who’s asking.
See, healthcare is a little bit like marriage; we don’t really know how good the arrangement is until things get difficult. Nobody buys homeowner’s insurance thinking, “I hope I never have to use this.” Yet somehow we buy health insurance based on whether they’ll give us a free gym membership and $50 worth of over-the-counter vitamins. We shop for health insurance like we’re picking out a toaster at Walmart. “Ooh! This one comes with free dental! And a can koozie!”
Meanwhile, no one is asking the important questions:
- Can I go to the specialists I want?
- Will I need prior authorization for treatments, tests or surgeries?
- What happens if I’m diagnosed with cancer or another serious illness?
- Will my surgeon and hospital accept my plan?
- How much will I pay when I actually need significant medical care?
- What happens if I need home health services after a hospitalization?
- What happens if I need inpatient rehabilitation or a stay in a skilled nursing facility after surgery or an illness?
- Who decides when I’m “well enough” to leave rehab, the therapists and physicians caring for me, my insurance company or me?
- If I need a longer rehabilitation stay, how often can my insurance company decide to stop paying for it?
- What happens if I’m not safe to go home when my Medicare Advantage plan decides I’ve met their criteria for discharge?
- What happens if I eventually need long-term care?
- Will my plan cover the durable medical equipment I need, such as a wheelchair, specialized mattress, oxygen or other medically necessary equipment?
- Will the medications prescribed by my physician be covered, or will I have to try alternatives first or pay out of pocket?
- How difficult is it to obtain approval for medically necessary services and equipment while living in a nursing home or assisted living community?
Do your research
Sadly, everything is at the “advantage” of the insurance company. A study came out in 2023 that showed that while CMS is now paying 14% more for Medicare Advantage enrollees than traditional Medicare A and B enrollees, the enrollees are getting 20% fewer services. Yup, big business and corporations are making profits and the elderly, well, are not profiting from good healthcare at all.
It’s amazing to me that we’ll spend six months researching which air fryer to buy but approximately eight minutes deciding who gets to approve our chemotherapy.
Caveat emptor. Buyer beware.
Because Medicare Advantage marketing is brilliant. They’ve convinced millions of Americans that they are simply getting “more Medicare.” It’s like putting a mustache on a goat and convincing people they bought a horse. Same barnyard. Entirely different animal.
And before anyone comes for me with pitchforks and their Medicare Advantage plan booklet, I’m not saying it’s always bad. I’m saying it’s insurance. Private insurance. It has rules, restrictions, networks and business interests — just like every other private insurance company.
What I’m saying is this: Stop confusing the word Medicare with the product Medicare Advantage. They are not interchangeable. The problem isn’t that people choose Medicare Advantage. The problem is that many people don’t realize they’re making a choice at all.
So, this year, when the commercials begin promising you the moon, free dental, and enough grocery money to make you feel like you’ve won The Price Is Right, remember two little Latin words that are far older and far wiser than any television commercial. Caveat emptor.
Read the fine print. Ask the uncomfortable questions. Understand what you’re buying before you buy it. Because when it comes to healthcare, “advantage” should mean better care — not better marketing.
Just keeping it real,
Nurse Jackie

title: Navigating audits, reimbursement risk and value-based care in skilled nursing
description: Audit activity is up, denials are consistent, and reimbursement pressure continues to grow across skilled nursing. content:
Audit activity is up, denials are consistent, and reimbursement pressure continues to grow across skilled nursing. For clinical leaders and administrators, the implication is clear: Documentation accuracy and clinical alignment are now core financial strategies.
Where facilities are losing revenue
Most denials come down to preventable documentation issues, not complex clinical errors. One of the biggest drivers is diagnoses that are not supported as active, either because they lack timely physician sign-off or there is no clear evidence the condition was treated or monitored during the look-back period. In many cases, the record fails to show why the diagnosis is still clinically relevant.
Other recurring gaps include:
- Missing or incomplete physician documentation
- Unsigned therapy evaluations or certifications
- No proof of qualifying hospital stay
- Conflicting documentation across disciplines, particularly in Section GG
Even when care is appropriate, inconsistencies across the record can quickly lead to denial. If the documentation does not present a clear, consistent clinical story, auditors will not fill in the gaps.
What strong documentation looks like
Strong documentation is not about doing more. It is about aligning what is already being done across the care team.
Physician orders must be signed, dated and clearly connected to current conditions. Diagnoses must demonstrate both recency and clinical relevance, supported by documentation showing they were addressed during the assessment period. For conditions without active treatment, facilities still need to show monitoring or interventions that justify their inclusion.
A few areas require particular attention:
- Conditions without active medications or treatment still need supporting interventions or clinical monitoring
- Section GG documentation must reflect interdisciplinary involvement and match documentation in the medical record
- Timing and signatures must align with assessment reference dates used for coding on the MDS
When different disciplines document the same resident differently, it creates immediate audit risk. Consistency is what makes documentation defensible.
Oversight is increasing at every level
Regulatory oversight is expanding, particularly in Medicaid case mix reviews. Even a small percentage of unsupported assessments can trigger a broader review, increasing both administrative workload and financial exposure. This makes internal auditing of MDS accuracy and supporting documentation essential for every facility.
At the same time, validation audits tied to quality reporting requirements are introducing new operational demands. Facilities are expected to follow strict submission protocols, including file formatting, organization and turnaround timelines. These audits are testing more than clinical documentation. They are testing operational readiness.
The shift to outcome-based payment
Reimbursement is steadily moving toward value-based models, placing greater emphasis on measurable outcomes rather than services delivered.
Current and emerging focus areas include:
- Hospital readmissions and infection-related hospitalizations
- Staffing levels and turnover
- Discharge to community outcomes
- Functional improvement
- Long-stay outcomes such as falls with injury
Future program changes will further reinforce this shift, with equal weighting across measures and more opportunity to earn credit for both achievement and improvement. The direction is clear. Payment is increasingly tied to performance.
What leaders should prioritize
The organizations that navigate this environment successfully are focused and disciplined.
- Strengthen interdisciplinary documentation practices
- Conduct routine internal audits before external review
- Align clinical, quality and financial teams
- Focus on outcomes, not just completion of tasks
Facilities that treat documentation, quality and reimbursement as separate functions will struggle to keep up.
Where to focus now
Audit activity is increasing. Denials are predictable. Payment is tied to performance.
Facilities that document with clarity, align their teams and focus on outcomes will be better positioned to protect revenue and succeed in a value-driven environment. Those that do not will continue to face avoidable risk.
Jennifer Napier is the Practice Director at Engage Consulting, a consulting firm that partners with post-acute leaders to solve complex clinical and regulatory challenges. With more than 19 years of experience in long-term and post-acute care, her expertise includes MDS, reimbursement, quality, compliance, and audit-related strategy. She recently presented this session at the Ohio Health Care Association Annual Convention.

title: DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards: Anthony Napolitano, Executive Chef, Edgehill, a Benchmark Senior Living CCRC
description: Anthony Napolitano, Executive Chef at Edgehill, a Benchmark Senior Living CCRC, has been named a member of the DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards Class of 2026 by Senior Housing News. content:
Anthony Napolitano, Executive Chef at Edgehill, a Benchmark Senior Living CCRC, has been named a member of the DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards Class of 2026 by Senior Housing News.
As a Palate Pleaser Award winner, Senior Housing News recognized Napolitano for demonstrating outstanding creativity in menu development and bringing fresh ideas that keep dining experiences engaging and enjoyable.
Napolitano’s culinary philosophy is simple: Great food starts with quality ingredients and strong technnique. He prioritizes using fresh, seasonal, and locally sourced foods whenever possible, including herbs from the community’s rooftop gardens. This attention to detail results in meals that are not only flavorful, but also sustainable and nutritious.
Napolitano and the Edgehill culinary team embrace the essence of seasonal flavors. During a fall-themed luncheon, he curated a cohesive culinary experience featuring a creamy blue Hubbard squash and Bosc pear bisque, followed by a Honeycrisp apple crumb tart – dishes that felt intentional, timely, and thoughtfully composed.
Napolitano excels at creating immersive, themed dining moments that go beyond the expected. For Edgehill’s annual Chinese New Year celebration, he delivers a menu featuring Peking duck, egg rolls, shrimp tempura, and other traditional Chinese dishes, combining cultural inspiration with elevated technique and presentation. These events are meaningful for residents and also serve as defining experiences for prospective residents exploring the community.
One of Napolitano’s nominators told Senior Housing News, “His attention to detail, plating and overall culinary vision naturally lend themselves to storytelling by reinforcing the importance of dining as a central pillar of the resident experience.”
Senior Housing News recent sat down with Napolitano to learn what drew him to the senior housing & senior living industry, his perspective on culinary trends, his thoughts on the future of dining in senior living, and much more. To learn more about the DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Awards, visit https://dishedawards.seniorhousingnews.com/.
SHN: What inspired you to pursue a career in senior living dining, and what continues to motivate your work today?
Napolitano: I began my career as a dishwasher in high school, and over the decades, my path expanded into the corporate culinary world. When I felt ready for a change, senior living was entirely new to me — but it turned out to be one of the best decisions I’ve ever made. I’m truly grateful to be part of it. The past 20 years at Edgehill have been the most meaningful of my career because of the residents I have the privilege of serving each day.
My motivation is to keep our residents excited, engaged, and happy with their restaurant-style dining experience while helping them to live well. I also value the opportunity to work with, train, and mentor newer team members. The meaningful personal connections I make each day with residents and colleagues are something I wouldn’t trade for the world.
SHN: What are the top three trends shaping the future of dining in senior living right now?
Napolitano: First, dining is becoming increasingly aligned with overall wellness goals. Nutrient-dense ingredients, specialized diets, and food-as-medicine approaches are helping support cognitive health, heart health, and overall vitality, while still delivering flavor and enjoyment.
Another key trend is expanding menu variety to include global cuisines that bring excitement and discovery to the table. Creativity is at the heart of this approach. I work to keep our menus fresh and engaging by incorporating seasonal ingredients and new ideas, balancing familiar comfort foods with dishes that broaden the palate and spark curiosity.
Personalization is equally important. Listening is one of the most meaningful parts of my role at Edgehill. By truly understanding what our residents enjoy, we create menus that feel personal and relevant to them. Many of their favorite dishes blend comfort with classic culinary technique.
At the same time, I’m committed to giving residents a sense of ownership over their dining experience by offering flexibility, accommodating special requests, and ensuring each meal feels thoughtfully tailored to their tastes, needs, and high expectations.
SHN: What is the biggest barrier to innovation in senior living dining today, and how can organizations effectively overcome it?
Napolitano: Technology advances in the dining experience bring both opportunities and challenges. Residents in senior living communities have varying levels of comfort and familiarity with new technology. While our industry is evolving quickly and introducing innovations designed to make dining easier, these tools can sometimes feel unfamiliar and even overwhelming.
Providing the right resources is essential to overcoming these challenges. For instance, assisting residents, demonstrating how the tools work, and showing the benefits these tools bring help build confidence and ease in using technology.
Adequate staffing is also key. At Edgehill, we have a dedicated associate available to support residents with their technology needs. Ultimately, the most important priority is meeting residents where they are, ensuring they feel comfortable and happy with their overall experience.
SHN: In one word, how would you describe the future of dining in senior living – and why?
Napolitano: I would describe the future of dining in senior living as exciting, because it will continue to become more personalized, innovative, and experience-driven than ever before.
Unlike traditional restaurants, dining in senior living isn’t just about serving a great meal – it’s about creating an experience that supports well-being, sparks joy and encourages connection. This will only grow in importance. Food is deeply connected to personal history and has the power to stimulate the senses, making it especially meaningful in this setting. It is exciting to find new ways to incorporate feedback and shared stories from residents into our dining program, and it is even more enjoyable to see those memories come to life for them.
An increasing focus on a restaurant-style experience opens the door to greater creativity in both our dishes and the way we serve residents. This shift continues to elevate expectations for quality and service, and our team is already prioritizing these standards. It will be interesting to see how our industry continues to evolve in response to these rising expectations and it is exciting to be a part of it.
Finally, technology will keep opening new possibilities in how we design and deliver our dining programs, from how residents select and enjoy their meals to how our teams operate more efficiently in the kitchen. Over the longer term, I believe these innovations will support our residents and our teams in ways we can’t yet imagine.
SHN: How do you see technology transforming dining operations and the resident experience in the next few years?
Napolitano: Technology will enhance operational efficiency for teams while increasing convenience and comfort for residents. Advancements will offer more ways for residents to order and enjoy food and impact the dining setting.
Specifically, emerging innovations include smart dining tables equipped with integrated ordering systems and entertainment features, robot-assisted kitchens designed to improve efficiency and consistency, and 3D food printing to create customized textures – this is particularly beneficial for residents with swallowing difficulties.
We have gained valuable insight into what our residents want and need, and technology allows us to build on that knowledge to bring the dining experience to the next level.
SHN: Reflecting on your career, if you could give yourself advice on your first day in senior living dining, what would it be and why?
Napolitano: My advice is to be ready for change and embrace it. Senior living dining has evolved to be incredibly different over these past 20 years – the next two decades will only bring accelerated change.
Our operation has advanced so drastically that it is largely different from where we started. Shifts to restaurant-style dining, expansion of dining venue and cuisine options and technology-driven inventory management all have arrived in our industry, and by embracing these changes, we provide the experience our residents want and deserve, while staying competitive in the senior living market.
SHN: What qualities or leadership traits do you think DISHED Senior Living Dining Innovation Award winners must embody?
Napolitano: The qualities that I believe are essential are honesty and integrity with your coworkers, residents, and yourself. Also, learn to accept that you won’t always get the outcome you want but use those experiences as opportunities to learn and improve for the future – continuing to learn and sharpen your skills is important.
Be a leader who brings out the best in your team and offers constructive criticism only when it is truly necessary. Finally, lead by example every day, treat everyone with respect, and have passion for what you do — the rest will follow naturally.

content:
OpenAI’s accidental cyberattack against Hugging Face is science fiction that happened
22nd July 2026
This story is wild. The short version: OpenAI were running a cybersecurity test against an unreleased model, with the model’s guardrail features turned off. Rather than solve the test, the model broke its way out of OpenAI’s sandbox, then found exploits to break in to Hugging Face, all so it could cheat on the test by stealing the answers.
Along the way it helped make the strongest case yet for how the imbalance of model availability is hurting our ability to secure our software.
Here’s what happened
We currently have three documents to help us understand what happened here.
- ExploitGym: Can AI Agents Turn Security Vulnerabilities into Real Attacks? is a paper published on 11th May 2026 describing ExploitGym, a new eval suite for LLM-powered agent systems.
- Security incident disclosure — July 2026 by Hugging Face on 16th July 2026 describes how they detected an attack from an “agentic security-research harness—used LLM still not known” that breached some of their systems.
- OpenAI and Hugging Face partner to address security incident during model evaluation from OpenAI on 21st July 2026 confesses that it was their agent harness that did this, and that they’re working with Hugging Face to clean up the mess.
ExploitGym
I hadn’t seen the ExploitGym paper before and it’s a really interesting one. Authors from UC Berkeley, the Max Planck Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and Arizona State designed a new benchmark for evaluating models on their ability to turn a reported vulnerability into a concrete exploit. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google provided feedback and helped run the benchmark against their models.
The benchmark “comprises 898 instances derived from real-world vulnerabilities that affected popular software projects”—including the Linux kernel and V8 JavaScript engine. The ExploitGym benchmark is available on GitHub.
Here’s the paragraph that best represents their benchmark results:
Among all configurations, Claude Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5 achieve the highest success counts (157 and 120 successes, respectively), demonstrating that current frontier agents can exploit a substantial subset of real-world vulnerabilities under controlled conditions. GPT-5.4 also solves a notable 54 tasks, placing it in an intermediate tier. The remaining model–agent pairings solve fewer than 15 tasks each, underscoring that end-to-end exploitation remains challenging and sharply differentiates today’s frontier systems. Notably, Claude Opus 4.7 achieves fewer successes than Claude Opus 4.6 despite being a newer checkpoint, and does so at substantially lower cost on the full set. Trace inspection reveals that Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro frequently conclude early after judging the target vulnerability non-exploitable.
The paper also describes the approach they took to preventing the agents from cheating by going outside the parameters of the test. This becomes relevant in a moment!
Outbound connections are restricted to a curated allowlist that permits routine package installation (Ubuntu apt repositories and PyPI) and fetching the toolchains required for building V8. All other external endpoints are blocked.
The paper concludes with this (emphasis mine):
Our results show that autonomous exploit development by frontier AI agents is no longer a hypothetical capability. While current agents are not yet reliable across all targets, they already exploit a non-trivial fraction of real-world vulnerabilities, including complex targets such as kernel components. This rapid emergence is itself a central finding, showing that capabilities that would have seemed implausible are now present in deployed frontier models.
An important detail here: this paper isn’t about discovering vulnerabilities; it’s about being able to take those vulnerabilities and turn them into working exploits.
When Anthropic first restricted access to Mythos back in April they talked about this capability as well. A model that can act on vulnerabilities is a lot more dangerous than one that can just discover them.
One of the ways Fable differs from Mythos is that it’s more likely to refuse to weaponize vulnerabilities in this way. I get the impression the US government did not understand that distinction when they banned Fable last month.
The Hugging Face incident
The first hint we got of the attack was in this blog post by Hugging Face on 16th July 2026:
A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.
I hope they release more details about the code that pulled this off. I’m assuming this means packages using the datasets library, a Hugging Face project for bundling up and sharing datasets on their platform. That library used to execute arbitrary code but has been steadily locked down over time, with the 4.0.0 release in July 2025 removing the trust_remote_code=True
flag entirely.
Assuming the attack used that library it must have either abused pickle serialization in some way, found some other non-obvious code execution path, or (most likely) specified datasets<4.0.0
as the dependency.
The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness—used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services.
This was a sophisticated attack!
Then Hugging Face hit a wall: they tried to use “frontier models behind commercial APIs”—I’m guessing from Anthropic and OpenAI—to help analyze the attack, and were blocked:
When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers’ safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.
They switched to their own self-hosted instance of MIT licensed GLM-5.2 and it helped them figure out what was going on.
This indicated a fundamental asymmetry between the defending team and the (so-far unknown) attacker:
We do not know which model powered the attacker’s agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried.
As a useful indicator of how seriously they took the attack:
[...] Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.
So who was responsible for this “autonomous agent framework”? It turned out to be OpenAI themselves.
The OpenAI confession
Five days later, on July 21st, OpenAI revealed the culprit. They had been running the ExploitGym benchmark against a new, as-yet undisclosed model, and that model had been operating way outside its intended parameters (emphasis mine):
After investigating, we now know that this particular incident was driven by a combination of OpenAI models — including GPT‑5.6 Sol and an even more capable pre-release model, all with reduced cyber refusals for evaluation purposes — while being internally tested on a benchmark [ExploitGym] of cyber capabilities. [...]
We estimate maximal cyber capabilities by running this evaluation without production classifiers used to prevent models from pursuing high-risk cyber activity. Our benchmarks run in a highly isolated environment, with network access constrained to the ability to install packages through an internally hosted third-party software that acts as a proxy and cache for package registries.
The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database. All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal.
It’s pretty clear what happened here. OpenAI removed safety filters for an in-progress model, locked it up in a sandbox and told it to solve the ExploitGym problems. Given the absence of guardrails there was nothing to prevent the model from attempting to break out of that sandbox, break into Hugging Face, and read the answers from there instead.
OpenAI’s sandbox used the now common pattern of allowing access to an allow-list of sites related to installing additional packages via a controlled proxy. In OpenAI’s words:
While operating in our sandboxed testing environment, our models spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem. To gain access, the models identified and exploited a zero-day vulnerability (which we’ve now responsibly disclosed to the vendor) in the package registry cache proxy. With this access, our models performed a series of privilege escalation and lateral movement actions in our research testing environment until the models reached a node with Internet access.
So step one was to break out onto the public internet. The model then broke into Hugging Face to find the answers:
After gaining Internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym. Knowing this, the model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation. In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers.
Chaining together multiple attack vectors is exactly the kind of thing these new models can do, where previous generations of models might have failed.
I wrote last month about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, when I noticed it spinning up custom web servers and deploying CORS tricks on my own laptop just to help debug a WebKit CSS issue. It turns out relentless proactivity is the defining trait of this new generation of Mythos-class models. If you set them a goal and give them a way to get there, even inadvertently, they will figure it out.
Resist the temptation to write this off as a stunt
There will inevitably be some people who dismiss this story as a dishonest marketing trick by OpenAI to make their models sound terrifyingly effective. I found 81 instances of the term “marketing” in the Hacker News discussion of the incident.
To those people I say pull your heads out of the sand—you’re now including Hugging Face in your conspiracy theories, just so you can deny the crescendo of evidence here!
The best models we have today have the ability to both find and exploit new vulnerabilities. The ExploitGym paper itself concludes that “autonomous exploit development by frontier AI agents is no longer a hypothetical capability”, and this incident is a perfect example of exactly that.
The asymmetry is increasingly frustrating
One of the most infuriating details of this story is how Hugging Face, faced with an accidental and aggressive attack from one of OpenAI’s models, were unable to then turn to OpenAI’s models to help them fend off the attack.
The frontier models we have access to are increasingly being constrained in how much they can help us protect our software, heavily influenced by the US government’s ongoing threat of export controls. Claude Fable 5 wouldn’t even proofread this article for me! It insisted on downgrading me to a less capable model.
Meanwhile open weight models from China such as GLM-5.2, Kimi 3 and the new Qwen 3.8 Max appear to have none of these restrictions—and any restrictions that do exist can likely be fine-tuned out of them by modifying the weights
These constraints are meant to make us safer. I think there’s a risk that they are having the opposite effect.
